Selectors

Selectors do not exist in because state is finalized, normalized, and exposed as immutable snapshots through reactive consumption surfaces rather than derived post hoc from a mutable store.

In selector-based architectures, state is often treated as a raw container from which values are derived later using memoized projection functions. takes a different approach: all value derivation occurs before state commitment, and the State stage emits a single, authoritative snapshot representing the completed result of pipeline execution.

doesn’t need selectors because state is always already there—fully resolved, immutable, and reactively available through the Vault. Once a pipeline execution completes, a single, authoritative state snapshot is committed and exposed globally, making derived projection layers unnecessary. Consumers observe state directly via .state, .state$, or framework-native reactive bindings, without indirection or memoization.

Where Selector Logic Lives in SDuX

In selector-based architectures, derived values are computed after state has been committed by projecting over a mutable store. does not support this model.

All value derivation in occurs before state commitment, inside the pipeline. The State stage emits a single, finalized, immutable snapshot that is already normalized and ready for consumption.

As a result, there is no selector layer. Consumers instead observe authoritative state snapshots directly through reactive or synchronous access surfaces.

Recommended References

  • State Stage — where finalized, immutable state snapshots are committed and emitted
  • Resolve Behaviors — where asynchronous, deferred, and promise-based inputs are resolved and normalized
  • Operator Behaviors — where resolved values may be conditionally forwarded, refined, or suppressed before downstream stages
  • Filter Behaviors — where resolved pipeline values may be conditionally excluded from further processing
  • Reducer Behaviors — where resolved values are deterministically reduced into the next state snapshot

Engineers migrating from selector-based systems should treat pipeline operators and resolve behaviors as the replacement for selector logic, and state consumption surfaces as the replacement for selector consumption.

Reactive State Projection (Selector Replacement)

Although does not provide a traditional selector layer, engineers will still often need to transform finalized state into shapes that are convenient for rendering, composition, or downstream consumption. That need does not disappear — it simply moves to a more reactive, deterministic place.

In , state transformation is bolted onto state emission rather than pulled from a store on demand. Instead of computing derived values through synchronous projection functions, engineers attach transformation logic to reactive state outputs and allow derived values to update automatically as state changes.

This model shifts state consumption from pull-based derivation to push-based projection. Finalized, immutable state snapshots are emitted by the Vault, and consumers react to those emissions by mapping, filtering, or combining state streams to produce consistent, application-specific shapes.

In practice, this means treating .state$ (or framework-native reactive bindings) as the attachment point for transformation logic. Derived values remain reactive, memoization is handled naturally by the reactive system, and all projections stay synchronized with the authoritative state snapshot.

By projecting from emitted state rather than querying a mutable store, preserves its core guarantees: immutability, determinism, and a single source of truth — while still giving engineers full control over how state is shaped and consumed throughout the application.

Note

does not provide a dedicated post-processing or selector stage inside the Vault. This is intentional. Introducing a formal selector layer would require additional scaffolding, lifecycle rules, and indirection to manage derived state within the pipeline itself.

Instead, encourages engineers to transform immutable state snapshots outside of the Vault, directly on reactive state emissions. This approach keeps the core pipeline simple and deterministic while giving engineers full flexibility to shape data using familiar, ergonomic patterns in their own code.

Examples: Reactive State Projection

In selector-based systems, derived state is typically computed by pulling from a store on demand. In , derived values are instead bolted onto reactive state emission. State is pushed by the Vault, and consumers project it into the shapes they need.

The examples below demonstrate how common selector-style transformations are implemented as reactive projections in Angular, React, and Vue.

Example: Reactive State Projection

In Angular, FeatureCell state is exposed as reactive signals. Derived values are expressed using computed(), which automatically re-evaluates when the underlying state snapshot changes.

In other frameworks, derived values are created by mapping the reactive state$ stream. The projection updates automatically whenever the Vault emits a new immutable state snapshot. 

{{`
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
@FeatureCell`}}<Employee[]>{{`('employees')
export class EmployeeService {
  readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  // Base reactive state
  readonly employees = this.vault.state.value;

  // Selector replacement: derived, reactive projection
  readonly activeEmployees = computed(() =>
    this.employees()?.filter(e => e.active) ?? []
  );

  constructor() {
    this.vault.initialize();
  }
}
`}}
 
{{`
employeeCell.initialize();

// Selector replacement: push-based projection
const activeEmployees$ = employeeCell.state$.pipe(
  map(({ snapshot }) =>
    snapshot.value?.filter(e => e.active) ?? []
  )
);

// Subscribe or bind into your reactive layer
activeEmployees$.subscribe(active => {
  console.info('Active employees:', active);
});
`}}

In all cases, the derived value reacts to state changes automatically. There is no pull-based querying, no selector registry, and no additional lifecycle to manage — projections remain synchronized by design.
